NEW DELHI: Promising to dissolve fat cells may sound like an attractive pitch for a slimming product, but it has landed FatX Solution in trouble with the country's drug regulator. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cancelled the product's registration after finding that it was being promoted with claims that are not permitted for cosmetics.In an order dated October 28, CDSCO said Delhi-based importer Tekno Midas Aesthetics was marketing FatX Solution on its website as a product that could dissolve fat cells and reduce their size. The regulator said these were drug-related claims and did not fit the definition of a cosmetic under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.The action followed a scrutiny of the company's application and website, during which CDSCO found differences between the claims being made online and those mentioned on the approved product label.Under the Cosmetics Rules, 2020, cosmetic products cannot make false or misleading claims. The rules define cosmetics as products meant for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance.Claims to dissolve fat cells go beyond this definition, the regulator said.CDSCO had issued a show-cause notice to the company on August 10, citing violations of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and the Cosmetics Rules. The company submitted its response on September 1, but the regulator found it inconclusive and unsatisfactory. The firm also requested that its registration certificate be voluntarily surrendered.Rajan Bhatnagar of Tekno Midas Aesthetics told TOI that the product had been registered as a cosmetic more than four years ago. "At that time, the licence was granted because the product was registered as a cosmetic. The authorities have now changed their interpretation of the category under which the product falls. Earlier, it was considered a cosmetic, but now they say it falls under another category," he said.He said the company had decided not to contest the matter after receiving the notice. "We did not want to get into any dispute or challenge the notification. We voluntarily requested the surrender of the licence, and the authorities cancelled it," he said.The Central Licensing Authority subsequently cancelled the registration certificate, RC/COS-003300, which was issued in July 2022 and was valid until July 14, 2027. The cancellation took effect from October 28.
Article Summary: FatX Solution was marketed as a product that could dissolve fat cells and reduce their size. The product's registration has been cancelled by the country's drug regulator. CDSCO said the claims were drug-related and did not fit the definition of a cosmetic.

Article Title: CGHS cover for dependent widowed, divorced daughters after parents' death
Article Text: Widowed and divorced daughters returning to live with parents can now be added to their parents' Central Govt Health Scheme (CGHS) cards, even after the death of the govt employee or pensioner in whose name the original card was issued. Health ministry has allowed eligible daughters to be added or reinstated in cards held by family pensioners.The move will help parents supporting daughters with no independent income who need medical care. Earlier, once the original cardholder died and the spouse began receiving family pension, there was no provision to add or reinstate dependent family members.The ministry said it had received representations from pensioners facing difficulties supporting such daughters, particularly those with serious medical conditions requiring continued treatment. The benefit will not be automatic: authorities will verify daughter's marital status, income and dependency.All other CGHS eligibility conditions will continue to apply, the Oct 28 order said. It has been circulated to all central govt ministries and departments and DG of CGHS.
Article Summary: Widowed and divorced daughters returning to live with parents can now be added to their parents' Central Govt Health Scheme (CGHS) cards, even after the death of the govt employee or pensioner in whose name the original card was issued. The move will help parents supporting daughters with no independent income who need medical care.

Article Title: PM lauds space scientists for successful launch of NVS-03; Isro chief says 2 more navigation sats to be launched to bolster constellation
Article Text:
PM Modi hailed Isro’s successful NVS-03 launch as a boost to NavIC, while the space agency plans two more navigation satellite launches in the coming months

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: With Isro successfully launching navigation satellite NVS-03, which carries an indigenously manufactured atomic clock, on Friday night from Sriharikota, PM Narendra Modi on Saturday called the GSLV-F18 mission “an important step in strengthening NavIC, our indigenous satellite navigation system”.Lauding Isro and its scientists, Modi said the “dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists continue to make our nation proud”. “Equipped with enhanced capabilities, NVS-03 will further our pursuit of self-reliance in critical technologies and support navigation services that benefit our people,” he further said on X on Saturday.Space minister Jitendra Singh said that “this remarkable achievement reflects India’s growing prowess in space technology and our unwavering commitment to strengthening sovereign indigenous navigation capabilities”.The success of the NVS-03 satellite mission will not only get India’s navigation system up and running again but also give a big boost to strategic forces as they have until now been dependent on foreign navigation systems like American GPS and Russian GLONASS for weapon and missile navigation.The advanced satellite has an indigenously developed atomic clock, which is the most accurate timekeeping device in the world.India has mastered this sophisticated technology and the desi atomic clock is now ticking in NVS-03 satellite in space.NavIC was until now not being used by the armed forces for the purposes of missile navigation, precise positioning and coordination of warships at sea, and indigenous navigation support for troop movement and combat aircraft. This is because four operational satellites were required for a standalone GPS-style position tracking system to work. The strategic forces were, therefore, dependent on foreign navigation systems. But the successful launch of NVS-03 has changed everything. It will make the NavIC constellation operational not only for strategic use but also for civilian purposes across India and up to 1,500 km (930 miles) beyond the country’s geographical borders.Indian security forces need an operational NavIC to maintain strategic autonomy and secure tactical advantage without relying on foreign-controlled networks. The four-satellite constellation will ensure secure, uncompromised communication, mobility and targeting data. Modern military hardware such as ballistic missiles and precision-guided munitions require highly accurate Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) signals to function effectively.Learning from past mistakes, Isro made an important change in the satellite system to make the launch successful. Isro chairman V Narayanan on Saturday revealed that in order to ensure mission reliability and bypass previous technical hurdles, the NVS-03 satellite was operated with “three pyro valves open”.Addressing the media at Sriharikota soon after the launch, Narayanan said that this bold technical decision was validated after rigorous vibration and shock testing by a national-level committee chaired by former Isro chief Kiran Kumar.Pyro valves are crucial in spacecraft propulsion. However, the NVS-02 satellite launched in 2025, the second spacecraft in the NVS series, was a failure due to a pryo valve-related problem. A high-level panel, after thorough analysis of the 2025 satellite failure, concluded that “the drive signal did not reach the pyro valve of the oxidiser line of the engine meant for orbit raising”.The Isro chief also informed that with four satellites, including NVS-01 now active in India's navigation satellite system, Isro plans to launch NVS-04 in five months, and NVS-05 in 10 months to further bolster the navigation satellite constellation.
Article Summary: PM Modi hails Isro’s successful NVS-03 launch as a boost to NavIC, while the space agency plans two more navigation satellite launches in the coming months. The advanced satellite has an indigenously developed atomic clock, which is the most accurate timekeeping device in the world.

Article Text:

What needs to change?

NEW DELHI: Animal testing remains an important part of pharmaceutical research, vaccine development and medical science in India. But a proposed overhaul of the rules governing laboratory experiments has triggered a debate over a fundamental question: Can India streamline scientific research without weakening safeguards for animals?The draft Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Control and Supervision of Experiment, Breeding and Trading of Laboratory Animals) Rules, 2026, issued by the Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA), proposes changes to how experiments are classified and approved. While it introduces a severity-based system for assessing animal suffering, animal welfare groups have raised concerns about reduced regulatory scrutiny, the use of certain animals and potential conflicts of interest in institutional approvals.The debate also comes at a time when advances in science are opening up alternatives to animal testing, including human cell-based studies, organoids, organ-on-chip technology and computer modelling. The question is whether India's regulatory framework is keeping pace with these developments.1.Experiments are categorized into four levels based on expected pain or distress: Mild, Moderate, Severe, Non-recovery2.An establishment's internal Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC) can directly approve mild and moderate experiments on any species.The central Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA) retains approval authority for severe and non-recovery procedures, specifically for animals positioned above rodents and rabbits.Replacement, Reduction and Refinement. These involve using alternatives wherever possible, limiting the number of animals to what is scientifically necessary and improving procedures and care to minimise suffering.The proposed framework also lays down requirements for the registration of establishments, institutional ethics committees, veterinary supervision, trained personnel and animal-care facilities. Experiments may be undertaken for specified purposes, including basic and applied research, drug and food safety testing, disease research, environmental protection and species conservationAnimal experimentation is not limited to pharmaceutical companies. Dr Surat, Senior Program Director, Research and Toxicology Department, Humane World for Animals India, said it is carried out across pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, medical research institutions, universities, veterinary colleges and government laboratories.Animals are used in vaccine development and batch testing, food and feed safety assessments, disease research and studies evaluating the effectiveness of potential treatments. Tests may assess short-term and long-term toxicity, skin and eye irritation, carcinogenicity and reproductive toxicity.Mice and rats are among the most commonly used laboratory animals, followed by rabbits, guinea pigs, fish and birds. Non-human primates are also used in certain areas of research.However, the scale of animal experimentation in India remains difficult to establish. Dr Surat said that although an estimated 100 million to more than 115 million animals are used in experiments and research worldwide every year, India does not have an official national figure or a transparent public database recording annual animal use, deaths and reported violations.Dr Ramanuj Panda, founder and managing director of Gocarin, has called for a centralised reporting system that records the species used, severity of experiments, animal deaths and welfare complaints.Animal experimentation in India is governed by the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960. The law provides for the CCSEA to regulate experiments and ensure that animals are not subjected to unnecessary pain or suffering.Section 17 requires the committee to ensure that animals are not subjected to unnecessary pain or suffering before, during or after experiments. Section 18 authorises inspections of facilities and examination of relevant records. Section 19 allows the committee to prohibit experiments where the rules are not being followed, subject to the prescribed process.The proposed rules would change how approval responsibilities are distributed, particularly for experiments involving mild and moderate levels of suffering.One of the major concerns raised by animal welfare organisations relates to provisions allowing certain experiments involving protected wild animals, wild-caught animals and stray or feral domestic animals, subject to specified conditions and permissions.PETA India has flagged these provisions, arguing that capturing, handling, transporting and confining animals not bred for laboratory use can cause distress and disrupt their natural behaviour. It has also questioned the scientific reliability of using animals whose health, genetic background and environmental histories may be unknown.The organisation has raised concerns about the possibility of community dogs and cats being exposed to laboratory use. It has also referred to a CCSEA circular issued in 2022 that allowed the use of stray dogs in certain vaccine trials. The circular was withdrawn in 2023.Dr Noopur Jain, Science and Research Policy Advisor at PETA India, said: "India should be moving towards modern, human-relevant non-animal science, not making animal experimentation easier."PETA has also argued that the severity of an experiment, rather than the size or species of the animal, should determine the level of regulatory scrutiny.Beyond the use of animals, the proposed shift towards institutional approvals has raised questions about independence and potential conflicts of interest.Dr Surat said five of the nine members of an IAEC belong to the same establishment seeking approval for an experiment, raising concerns about how independent research proposals may be assessed.The concern is that institutions could approve mild and moderate experiments involving a wider range of species without prior CCSEA clearance. This makes the role of independent members, veterinary supervision and clear scientific justification particularly important.Panda said streamlining approvals should not come at the cost of animal welfare. He called for meaningful participation by independent members in IAEC decisions, mandatory veterinary supervision, documented scientific justification and external reviews for experiments involving greater levels of suffering.The draft provides for inspections by designated nominees, including a socially aware member, at least twice a year. Separately, CCSEA inspection teams can inspect facilities to verify compliance.Dr Surat said facilities also undergo physical inspections for fresh registration and five-year renewals, while yearly mid-term inspections are mandated for large-animal research facilities.Another issue is whether India could become a destination for outsourced animal research.Dr Rukmini Jonnalagadda, founder and chief scientific officer of ULQA Scientific, Hyderabad, referred to an October 2026 investigation by Irish publication The Journal, which found that Irish universities had commissioned animal experiments at overseas laboratories, including in India.The University of Galway disclosed payments of €102,174 to an Indian organisation, Presude Lifesciences, for overseas studies.Ireland's Health Products Regulatory Authority confirmed that it has no regulatory role over animal experiments conducted abroad. The investigation does not establish that the Indian studies violated local rules, but it raises questions about how institutions commissioning research overseas assess and monitor animal welfare standards.Animal models can provide useful scientific information, but differences between species can limit how accurately they predict human responses. Animals and humans may process chemicals differently and have distinct genetic, metabolic, immune and physiological characteristics.Panda said animal research should not be treated as proof that a drug or treatment will be safe for people.One frequently cited example is the 2006 clinical trial of TGN1412, an antibody that had appeared safe in preclinical testing involving non-human primates. During the first human trial, all six healthy volunteers who received the antibody developed severe immune reactions.Dr Surat also pointed to gene therapy research for X-linked myotubular myopathy. Although the treatment showed promise in dog models, clinical trials in humans were associated with severe liver complications and deaths.He also cited safety concerns surrounding Sarepta Therapeutics' Elevidys gene therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which received a boxed warning from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) over serious liver injury.These cases do not mean animal research has no scientific value. They highlight the limitations of relying on animal studies as the sole predictor of human safety, particularly in complex diseases and therapies.New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) include cell-based tests, three-dimensional tissue cultures, organoids, organ-on-chip systems and computer-based models. These methods allow researchers to study aspects of human biology without relying on live animals at every stage of testing.Organoids are miniature structures grown from cells that mimic certain features of human organs, while organ-on-chip systems reproduce selected functions of organs. Computer models can also help predict how substances may behave in the human body.However, these methods cannot yet replicate every interaction between organs, the immune system and other biological processes in a whole organism. They are therefore being used alongside animal models in areas where complex biological interactions remain difficult to reproduce.India has taken some steps towards recognising alternatives. The New Drugs and Clinical Trials (Amendment) Rules, 2023, recognised methods such as cell-based assays, organ chips, microphysiological systems and computer modelling for relevant regulatory purposes.A government response to Parliament in 2026 highlighted support for 109 non-animal testing projects by the Indian Council of Medical Research across 71 institutions and laboratories.However, experts say wider adoption requires investment in infrastructure, training, validation and collaboration between researchers and regulators.Dr Surat argued that the draft rules should do more than classify experiments according to severity. India should consider stronger provisions to promote the development and validation of alternatives, including a requirement that animal procedures should not be undertaken where a recognised non-animal method is available.The proposed framework could be strengthened by requiring researchers to document their search for alternatives before seeking approval, publishing annual statistics on animal use and establishing a national centre to validate non-animal testing methods.Dr Surat also flagged ambiguity in the draft's definition of a "humane endpoint", the point at which an experiment should be stopped to prevent further suffering. The rules, the expert said, need to establish a clear and actionable response when an animal reaches that stage.Panda said experiments involving prolonged suffering should face strict scrutiny, with veterinary monitoring, appropriate pain relief and clearly defined humane endpoints. He added that a transition away from routine animal experimentation was possible in an increasing number of applications, but would require rigorous scientific validation and a clear regulatory pathway.Dr Surat also pointed to policy initiatives in the US, UK, European Union and China to advance human biology-based testing methods. India, the expert argued, would risk falling behind without comparable policy support and investment.The challenge is not simply to reduce the number of animals used in laboratories. It is to ensure that research is scientifically justified, animals are protected wherever experiments continue, and credible alternatives are developed and adopted wherever possible.As the government considers feedback on the draft rules, the central question remains whether the proposed framework can balance scientific research with stronger safeguards while creating a clearer path towards methods that are more relevant to human health.
Article Summary: The draft Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Rules, 2026, proposes changes to how experiments are classified and approved. It introduces a severity-based system for assessing animal suffering. Animal welfare groups have raised concerns about reduced regulatory scrutiny, the use of certain animals and potential conflicts of interest.

Six people were killed on Friday when a Trans Bharat Aviation helicopter flying from Badrinath to Dehradun crashed near Chai village in Uttarakhand's Chamoli district. The operator's fleet has been grounded and the cause is under investigation.The crash takes this year's toll in smaller civilian aircraft accidents to 22 deaths in six fatal accidents, the highest annual figure in a TOI compilation covering January 2021 to October 2026.Yet these deaths are a small part of India's transport toll. Roads kill more than 500 people every day. Major train accidents have fallen sharply, but thousands still die on railway tracks and premises. Scattered across individual incidents, many of these deaths receive little attention compared with major disasters.Road accidents killed 1,83,434 people in 2025, up 3.5% from 1,77,175 in 2024, according to provisional figures the road transport ministry gave Parliament. There were 5,13,474 crashes, about 1,407 a day. On average, 503 people died every day, nearly 21 every hour. The figures come from the government's Electronic Detailed Accident Report (e-DAR) portal as of July 27, 2026.Road deaths have risen every year since 2021, when 1,53,972 people were killed.The toll is up about 19% in four years. Crashes have also grown deadlier over the long term. Accident severity, measured as deaths per 100 reported accidents, rose from 21.6 in 2005 to 36.3 in 2024. Provisional figures indicate a slight dip to 35.7 in 2025.National highways make up only 2.1% of India's road network but accounted for 36.6% of road deaths in 2024, or 64,772 lives. Provisional figures show that highway deaths fell 4.1% to 62,122 in 2025, even as overall road fatalities rose.Uttar Pradesh recorded the most deaths in 2025 (27,547) and Tamil Nadu the most accidents (71,195). India has committed to halving road traffic deaths and injuries by 2030. The government has also announced a new rating system for national highways that will assess road conditions, safety and user experience.Consequential train accidents, which include collisions, derailments, fires and level-crossing accidents, fell from 135 in 2014-15 to 31 in 2024-25 and 16 in 2025-26, an 88% drop over 11 years. They killed 17 people in 2025-26, against 18 the year before.A single disaster can still be devastating. The Balasore triple-train collision in Odisha on June 2, 2023, killed 296 people and injured more than 1,200. Investigators identified signalling and interlocking lapses linked to the crash.The overall trend, however, is downward. Accidents per million train-kilometres fell from 0.11 to 0.01 between 2014-15 and 2025-26. The government credits improvements in signalling, track maintenance, rolling stock and safety technology, including the Kavach automatic train protection system. Spending and budget allocations for railway safety rose from Rs 39,200 crore in 2013-14 to Rs 1,17,693 crore in 2025-26.But far more people die around the railway network than in major train accidents.The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) recorded 22,413 deaths on railway tracks and premises in 2024, and another 1,888 at railway crossings, a total of 24,301. Of the 22,413 deaths on tracks and premises, 17,029 involved people falling from trains or being struck on the tracks. Maharashtra recorded the most deaths on railway tracks and premises in 2024 (3,587), followed by Uttar Pradesh (3,538). Separately, Government Railway Police data recorded 2,468 deaths on Mumbai's suburban railway network that year, down from 2,590 in 2023.Air crashes kill far fewer people overall. A July 2025 parliamentary reply counted 18 accidents involving Indian-registered scheduled aircraft since 2015. But a single disaster can claim hundreds. The Air India AI171 crash in Ahmedabad on June 12, 2025, killed 260 people: 241 aboard and 19 on the ground.Smaller aircraft are counted separately. A TOI review of accident reports, government records and news reports finds at least 60 deaths in 19 fatal accidents involving smaller civilian aircraft between January 2021 and October 2026. These involved helicopters, chartered aircraft, training planes, air ambulances and small regional passenger aircraft. The compilation excludes military aircraft and large commercial airliners.The annual toll was one death in 2021, 14 in 2022, four in 2023, five in 2024, 14 in 2025 and 22 so far in 2026. Helicopters accounted for 37 of the 60 deaths and fixed-wing aircraft for 23.This year's accidents span different kinds of operations. A passenger died after an IndiaOne Air aircraft made a forced landing near Rourkela in January. Later that month, a Learjet crash at Baramati killed five, including Maharashtra deputy chief minister Ajit Pawar In February, seven died in an air-ambulance crash in Jharkhand's Chatra district, and another passenger died after a Pawan Hans helicopter crash near Mayabunder in the Andamans. A training-aircraft crash near Kanpur killed two in August, followed by Friday's six deaths near Joshimath.The Baramati, Chatra and Joshimath crashes alone accounted for 18 of this year's 22 deaths.Uttarakhand accounted for 21 of the 30 helicopter-accident deaths in India during the preceding five years, or 70%, according to a July 2025 government reply in the Rajya Sabha. In TOI's compilation, 27 of the 60 deaths are linked to pilgrimage helicopter flights.The AAIB's final report on the June 2025 Gaurikund crash in Uttarakhand, which killed seven, cited rapidly descending clouds, delayed flight-path decisions and limited experience in the Kedarnath valley. It recommended 50 hours of supervised hill flying before pilots undertake single-pilot operations in the valley for the first time.Nationally, the helicopter accident rate rose from 0.33 per 10,000 flying hours in 2024 to 0.53 in 2025, although four accidents in 2025 are too few to establish a sustained deterioration in safety.Investigators also found visibility below the minimum for visual flying and faded runway markings at Baramati, and inadequate flight-data-monitoring records at the Kanpur flying school.These findings point to operational weaknesses, but they do not establish that smaller aircraft are inherently more dangerous than commercial airliners.At the 2025 average, India's roads claimed roughly as many lives every 12½ hours as the 260 people killed in the AI171 crash. A single average day's road toll was nearly 30 times the number killed in consequential train accidents in all of 2025-26. Air and train disasters bring immediate investigations and extensive coverage. Road deaths, spread across lakhs of crashes, rarely receive the same sustained attention.The railways show that sustained investment and safety measures can coincide with a sharp fall in major operational accidents. The challenge is to bring similar attention to road safety, deaths around railway tracks and the oversight of smaller aircraft, areas where prevention rarely draws the attention that disasters do.
Article Summary: Road accidents killed 1,83,434 people in 2025, up 3.5% from 1,77,175 in 2024. Road deaths have risen every year since 2021, when 1,53,972 people were killed. On average, 503 people died every day, nearly 21 every hour.

Article Title: Watch: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay launches one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns
Article Text:
Vijay presented 22-carat, one-gram gold rings to 25 newborns. (PTI)

Who is eligible for the gold ring?

Scheme draws on Tamil tradition

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. He also held some of the newborns and presented the rings to beneficiaries during the launch programme.Under the scheme, eligible babies born in government hospitals and government primary health centres will receive a 22-carat, one-gram gold ring.The initiative, named the Maternal Uncle Gold Ring Scheme (Thaaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam), has an annual allocation of Rs 755.83 crore.It is aimed at celebrating motherhood, promoting maternal and child health and encouraging institutional deliveries by increasing public confidence in government healthcare facilities.The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions.Mothers must be registered under the Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation (PICME) system and have a Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) ID. They will also have to provide an e-KYC-verified Aadhaar card along with one of the prescribed identity or residence documents.These include ration cards, voter identity cards, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates.The state government has already procured 1.28 lakh one-gram gold rings for the initial rollout. Each ring will have a unique serial number and will be packed in tamper-proof packaging.From Monday, babies born in government hospitals will receive the rings at the time of discharge, according to the state government.To clear the backlog of eligible babies born between June 22 and Monday, the government will distribute the rings through 107 hubs across Tamil Nadu.Distribution will begin at the rate of 100 babies per day at each hub. At designated centres, 25 beneficiaries will be accommodated in the morning and another 25 in the afternoon to avoid overcrowding, PTI reported.Village Health Nurses will distribute invitations informing beneficiaries of their allotted date and time. Beneficiaries have been asked to visit the designated centres only at the time mentioned in their invitations.The district administration has also made transportation arrangements for beneficiaries from their respective areas. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election as a symbolic gift to newborns, drawing on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’. The scheme has retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday.A government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of a child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.According to ANI, Tamil Nadu minister Arun Raj explained the cultural significance of the initiative saying, "A maternal uncle is someone who is among the first to rush in when a child is born, sharing in his sister’s happiness as his own. He assures her that he will always stand by her and her child, offering love, support and a sense of security.""Today, the Tamil Nadu Government, under the leadership of our brother, Mr. Vijay, is embracing this sacred bond of the maternal uncle and, as a gesture of that affection, is set to provide a one-gram gold ring to every child born in government hospitals. When the scheme was announced and the question arose as to where it should be launched, the place chosen by our Chief Minister was Madurai. This is the sacred soil of Madurai, blessed with the compassion and grace of Mother Meenakshi," he added.Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries annually, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or around 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.The government said the scheme is intended to encourage safe institutional deliveries, strengthen maternal and child welfare and increase public trust in government healthcare services.The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings based on annual requirements, while a project and programme management unit will oversee implementation and monitoring.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election.

Article Title: Delhi landfill garbage mountains shrinking, 100 acres reclaimed in 18 months: CM Rekha Gupta
Article Text:
Delhi CM Rekha Gupta poses for a group picture during an on-site inspection of waste disposal operations near Okhla, in New Delhi

Government targets legacy and fresh waste

New processing plants at three sites

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What is your top concern regarding pollution in Delhi? Landfill waste Air quality Water quality (Yamuna) Dust pollution 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Focus on pollution and waste management

NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed waste disposal work at Okhla and laid the foundation stone for new waste processing facilities at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola.Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years, with a large portion of the cleared area also being turned green.She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed."Today, at Okhla, we have processed almost all the legacy waste that was there before January 2025," Gupta said.Gupta said the government was working on two fronts: clearing the existing garbage mountains while ensuring that fresh waste generated every day did not accumulate into new landfill sites.According to news agency ANI, she said around 3,000-4,000 metric tonnes of fresh waste reaches the sites daily and is being processed round the clock."The garbage currently piled up here is essentially fresh waste generated after January 2025, and that too is being processed round the clock. So, we are fighting on two fronts: one is eliminating waste, and the other is ensuring that the 3,000 to 4,000 metric tons of fresh waste arriving daily is processed immediately, so that new garbage mountains are not formed for future generations," Gupta said.She said the government was working to reduce the existing garbage mountains to zero."People are seeing that the garbage mountains are continuously shrinking and soon a time will come when they will become zero," Gupta said.Gupta also said she had taken what she described as her "last selfie" with the garbage mountain at Okhla."Today I have taken my last selfie with the garbage mountain; after this I have taken a pledge that this garbage mountain will end soon," she said.Taking a jibe at the Opposition, Gupta added, "I had said - garbage mountain, you will have to go; the opposition mocked. Today I will say the garbage mountain is going; now only its back remains."During the programme at the Okhla SLF site, Gupta laid the foundation stone for fresh waste processing plants at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola, as well as a biogas facility at Ghazipur. She also inaugurated the M&CW Centre at Kotla Mubarakpur through virtual mode from Okhla.The Okhla plant will be built at a cost of Rs 103 crore and will have a processing capacity of 1,400 metric tonnes per day.The Singhola facility will cost Rs 42 crore and have a capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day, while the Ghazipur plant will have a processing capacity of 700 metric tonnes per day.The facilities are intended to process fresh waste as well as construction and demolition waste. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure."Waste should not remain waste; Delhi should use it as wealth," she said, adding that new technologies were being introduced for waste segregation and processing.She said waste and cattle dung would be used to produce biogas and manure as part of efforts to build a technology-driven waste management system.Gupta said the government was taking up several measures to address pollution, including work on landfill waste, cleaning the Yamuna, dust mitigation, plantation, road infrastructure and waste management."Our government is tackling pollution from a 360-degree perspective to ensure it gradually decreases. We are working on every aspect, be it addressing the mountains of garbage, cleaning the Yamuna, improving road infrastructure, or managing waste, to ensure the people of Delhi enjoy better air quality. Our resolve and policies are absolutely clear, and we are working 24x7 in the public interest," she said.The chief minister also reviewed the progress of waste disposal work with officials and directed them to accelerate the work according to the stipulated timeline.She said the garbage mountains at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla had caused inconvenience to people travelling through these areas and said the government was continuing efforts to eliminate them.
Article Summary: Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years. She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure.

Article Title: India-US trade talks hit ‘plateau’: Sitharaman says further give-and-take ‘very, very difficult’
Article Text:
Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman

India stresses strategic autonomy in trade negotiations

India-EU pact opens market access

India and US have reached a “plateau” in negotiations over their bilateral trade agreement, with further concessions from either side likely to be "very very difficult", finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi, she said that while negotiations are still underway, any progress from here would depend on whether there was limited room for compromise on either side.“The agreement negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” Sitharaman said.She said the agreement was still being “hard and very rigorously negotiated” and that India has a trade surplus with the US. “But what is the predominant feature of the trade relations between India and the US? The trade balance is very much in our favor.”Sitharaman said that the US would naturally want to reduce this trade imbalance and address what it sees as losses built up over the years.She also said that the way countries negotiate trade deals was changing, with governments now looking beyond traditional negotiations to address trade imbalances.“Negotiation used to be the only platform through which countries could highlight the discrepancies, highlight the lop-sidedness and say, would we want to correct this?” she said.“Tariff was an instrument of negotiation, and tariff had a certain framework within which you will apply it. Today framework is there, tariffs are going,” she said, while stressing that countries still need to negotiate and find “some give and take”.Sitharaman was also asked about maintaining strategic autonomy while negotiating bilateral trade agreements with European countries, including in the context of India procuring Russian oil."There is no Lindsay Graham Bill in Europe...," she said.On the broader question of how bilateral trade agreements can protect a country's interests in an era of multilateralism, Sitharaman said countries were increasingly choosing bilateral partnerships where they saw greater benefit.“Countries choose where multilateralism would benefit them, and there are some unique bilaterals which countries choose to have. The balance is somewhat tilted in favour of the bilateral rather than the multilateral,” she said.She said countries were now increasingly looking for new trade partners and strengthening those relationships through agreements.“Countries are now rapidly catching up with — I would put the EU-India also in a bilateral mode -because it's one in the name of union, but of course within them they have. So, bilaterals today are catching up far more than even initiating or beginning a multilateral. It's not deliberate, but in a way, if you don't do it, you're not moving forward. Countries will have to choose new partners for their trade and strengthen the tie through an agreement. And therefore, newer partnerships are being searched for, and they are tied up bilaterally.”FM Sitharaman cited the India-EU trade agreement as a major example of India's approach to negotiating trade pacts while protecting domestic interests.She said India had opened 92.5 per cent of its tariff lines and around 97 per cent of tariff value under the agreement. The EU, meanwhile, had opened 99 per cent in value terms and possibly 97 per cent of tariff lines.According to Sitharaman, greater access to the European market could support employment in labour-intensive sectors, including footwear, textiles, toys and processed products. Many of these sectors are linked to micro and small enterprises.“Those are all in the micro and small medium industry segment, which are labor-intensive,” Sitharaman said, adding that greater access to the European market could generate “more exports, more jobs”.Sitharaman said bilateral trade agreements were becoming increasingly important as multilateral institutions have weakened.“Multilateralism is not going to go away. But multilateralism has weakened,” she said.She also stressed that multilateralism should continue even as countries increasingly pursue bilateral agreements.“Multilateralism is not going to go away and multilateralism shouldn't go away,” Sitharaman said.The Munich Leaders Meeting, being held in the National Capital, provides a platform for about 100 senior decision-makers and experts to discuss opportunities for stronger cooperation among emerging and middle powers amid profound geopolitical change. Discussions include geoeconomic developments, trade and connectivity, maritime security, defence cooperation and other key international challenges.
Article Summary: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman says India and US have reached a 'plateau' in negotiations over their bilateral trade agreement. She said any progress from here would depend on whether there was limited room for compromise on either side. She also said the way countries negotiate trade deals was changing, with governments now looking beyond traditional negotiations to address trade imbalances.

Article Title: Jio IPO sees bumper demand: India's largest public issue fully subscribed in just 100 minutes of opening
Article Text:
The IPO is open to retail investors, employees and eligible Reliance shareholders.

Jio IPO

Jio IPO: Jio Platforms' $3.2 billion initial public offering (IPO) was fully subscribed within less than two hours of bidding opening on Wednesday, as investors rushed to participate in India's biggest-ever share sale. The offering is also the first IPO from billionaire Mukesh Ambani 's Reliance group in two decades.According to a PTI report, the Jio IPO was fully subscribed within 100 minutes of its opening on October 21.The rapid subscription was notable because large IPOs in India often see a slow start, with institutional investors typically placing their bids closer to the closing deadline. By comparison, the National Stock Exchange of India's share sale recently attracted subscriptions for just 42% of the shares on offer on its first day. Hyundai Motor India's IPO had received bids for only 18% of its offering on the opening day.Also Read | Jio IPO, India’s largest public issue, opens for subscription: Price band, GMP to brokerage views - top 10 things to know The IPO is open to retail investors, employees and eligible Reliance shareholders. The issue will close on Friday, with shares priced in a band of Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119 apiece.Exchange data showed that institutional investors had bid for 3.25 times the shares reserved for them by Wednesday. Retail participation was lower at that stage, with individual investors applying for 0.22 times their reserved quota.Retail investors have been allocated around one-third of the total offering.The IPO values Jio Platforms at as much as $108.3 billion. Once trading begins on October 28, the company could rank among India's largest listed companies by market capitalisation.Earlier this week, Jio Platforms allotted shares worth $853 million to domestic and international investors, including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and BlackRock. The anchor investor portion attracted bids exceeding $25 billion, according to a Reuters report.Backed by global investors such as Meta, Google's parent company Alphabet and other institutional investors, Jio Platforms houses India's largest telecom operator. With more than 500 million subscribers, the business is the world's second-largest telecom operator within a single country, behind China Mobile.This is Reliance's first IPO since 2006. Jio Platforms' telecom business, led by Ambani's son Akash, began operations in 2016. Its strategy was built around the expectation that Indians would use the internet much more extensively if access became almost free. By offering inexpensive data and free voice calls, Jio quickly gained market share from competitors such as Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea.
Article Summary: Jio IPO was fully subscribed within 100 minutes of its opening on October 21. The rapid subscription was notable because large IPOs in India often see a slow start. The IPO is open to retail investors, employees and eligible Reliance shareholders. The issue will close on Friday, with shares priced in a band of Rs 1,065 to Rs1,119 apiece.

Article Title: LPG consumption down, diesel & petrol sales up in September
Article Text:
LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier

NEW DELHI: LPG demand fell by over 9% year-on-year in Sept, while petrol and diesel sales registered growth of 7% and 5%, respectively, provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) showed.LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier.Month-on-month consumption, however, registered a growth of 8%, up from 2.4 MT.Petrol sales increased from 3.4 MT in Sept last year to 3.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose from 6.8 MT to 7.1 MT. Petrol and diesel consumption had registered year-on-year growth of 7.9% and 6.5%, respectively, in July.While petrol is largely used as an automobile fuel and its consumption is commensurate with the increasing number of vehicles, diesel is consumed by transport vehicles for passenger and freight movement, besides being used in the agricultural sector.Erratic monsoon conditions due to El Nino boosted demand for diesel for irrigation.Cumulative petrol consumption during Apr-Sept in the current financial year increased 7% to 22.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose 4.8% to 47.9 MT. In contrast, LPG consumption declined 14.9% to 13.8 MT from 16.2 MT during the corresponding period of 2025-26.
Article Summary: LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier. Petrol sales increased from 3.4 MT in Sept last year to 3.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose from 6.8 MT to 7.1 MT.

Article Title: 2,152 more AI cameras, 85% conviction rate: Amit Shah lauds Chandigarh Police on Raising Day
Article Text:
Union home minister Amit Shah being greeted by Punjab governor and Chandigarh administrator Gulab Chand Kataria during the '60th Raising Day event of Chandigarh Police'





CHANDIGARH: Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday announced that Chandigarh would get 2,152 additional AI-enabled surveillance cameras to strengthen the city’s security network.He also expressed confidence that Chandigarh Police would become the first police force in the country to achieve a drug-free status.Addressing police personnel at Chandigarh Police Lines in Sector 26 on the occasion of the force’s 60th Raising Day and the President’s Police Colour ceremony, Shah said the city had demonstrated how effective implementation of the three new criminal laws could speed up the criminal justice process and improve conviction rates.Chandigarh already has around 2,130 CCTV cameras installed across the city. The additional cameras, being provided by the Centre, would expand surveillance coverage and help police monitor suspicious activities and prevent crime, he said.Highlighting the force’s performance under the new criminal laws, Shah said 8,206 FIRs had been registered in Chandigarh since August 4, 2024. Online chargesheets had been filed in 7,590 cases, accounting for nearly 92.5% of the total.He said Chandigarh Police had recorded an overall conviction rate of around 85%, with the average time taken to secure convictions being 140 days. In cases registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, the conviction rate had reached 93%, he added.Shah said the figures showed how effective implementation of the new criminal laws could bring changes to the country's criminal justice system.He also praised Chandigarh Police’s campaign against drug trafficking and gangsters and expressed confidence that the city would lead the national drive against narcotics.The home minister highlighted the force’s emergency response capabilities, saying its average response time was four minutes, while quick response teams (QRTs) could reach a spot in around 10 minutes.He said the combination of technology, improved investigation and faster response would further strengthen public safety in the city.Shah also said 154 new vehicles had been added to the Chandigarh Police fleet in 2026 to improve patrolling, mobility and emergency response. Another 141 vehicles were announced for induction into the fleet.Congratulating the force on receiving the President’s Police Colour, Shah said the honour recognised six decades of discipline, dedication and service since Chandigarh Police was established in 1966.He urged police personnel to prioritise the fight against drugs and protect the younger generation from addiction, saying a drug-free Chandigarh would contribute to the larger goal of a developed India.
Article Summary: Chandigarh already has around 2,130 CCTV cameras installed across the city. The additional cameras, being provided by the Centre, would expand surveillance coverage and help police monitor suspicious activities and prevent crime. Online chargesheets had been filed in 7,590 cases, accounting for nearly 92.5% of the total.

Article Title: India ready to share its battle-tested expertise with Asean partners to boost joint capabilities: Rajnath
Article Text:
Defence minister Rajnath Singh addressing the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM)

Rajnath Singh with Australian and Japanese defence ministers

NEW DELHI: India’s extensive expertise in counter-terrorism is not theoretical classroom knowledge but it is an experience hard-earned on the ground through decades of directly confronting complex, cross-border security challenges, defence minister Rajnath Singh said in the Philippines on Thursday.Addressing the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) - Plus in Cebu, Rajnath underlined that “every strategy of India has been tested, refined and proven in the crucible of real-world operations” and that India stands fully prepared to share its practical, battle-tested experience with ADMM-Plus partners through joint exercises, capacity-building programmes, and robust intelligence sharing to strengthen collective capabilities. He reaffirmed the country’s commitment to collective regional security and eradication of terrorism in all its forms.Rajnath said this proactive, battle-tested doctrine was decisively demonstrated during Operation Sindoor, when India dismantled terrorist infrastructure and enforced a non-negotiable red line against state-sponsored terror. He stressed that counter-terrorism remains an important area of cooperation under the ADMM-Plus framework, and India and Malaysia are co-chairing the experts’ working group on counter-terrorism for the 2024 to 2027 cycle.Rajnath highlighted that by deploying frontline warships, India has successfully escorted thousands of merchant vessels and thwarted dozens of high-seas hijackings, extending protection to commercial shipping irrespective of flag or nationality. He termed the security of commercial shipping as India’s responsibility. “In an era where global trade routes face complex transnational threats, India stands ready to move beyond rhetoric. There is a need for effective action, regular operational presence and international cooperation. India will continue serving as a reliable net security provider in the Indian Ocean Region and the wider Indo-Pacific,” he said.The minister highlighted the importance of youth engagement in strengthening India-ASEAN defence cooperation, stating that the shared demographic profile and aspirations of the young populations provide a strong foundation for deeper regional partnership. He proposed the establishment of a dedicated defence ‘Youth Bridge’ to enhance institutional people-to-people connectivity, promote digital innovation and facilitate capacity building in line with ADMM-Plus initiatives.On the sidelines of ADMM-Plus, Rajnath met Japanese minister of defence Shinjiro Koizumi, and Australian minister for defence Richard Marles and posted a picture with them. “JAI: Japan, Australia, India”, the defence Minister posted on X, with him holding hands of both Marles and Koizumi, as he stood in the middle.At the forum, the minister reiterated that India attaches importance to ASEAN centrality and a secure, open, inclusive, resilient and rule-based Indo-Pacific, where peace and stability are not just aspirations but a result of collective commitment. He stated that its strategic engagement with ASEAN is long-term and rooted in shared interests, mutual respect and practical cooperation. He recalled that the second ASEAN-India defence ministers’ informal meeting in Kuala Lumpur in Oct last year reaffirmed the commitment to advancing the defence and security components of the ASEAN-India Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and the ASEAN-India Plan of Action for 2026 to 2030.On the theme of 13th ADMM-Plus ‘Navigating Our Future, Together’, Rajnath stated it resonates with India’s foreign and defence policy paradigms as well as its civilisational ethos of ‘Sarve Bhavantu Sukhinah’ (May all beings be happy) that reflects the aspiration for the happiness, prosperity, and well-being of all the people across the world. “This theme reminds us that our greatest strength lies in our solidarity and the shared ability to leverage our geographic, economic and strategic diversity. India believes in an international system built on mutual trust, co-operation, and collective responsibility. It is this precise collaborative spirit that empowers us to overcome the challenges to peace and order,” he said.The minister described maritime cooperation as crucial to India’s engagement with ASEAN during 2026, highlighting New Delhi’s designation of 2026 as the ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation and the conduct of the second ASEAN-India Maritime Exercise. He emphasised that India does not merely preach the tenets of international maritime law; it is a steadfast practitioner of global laws concerning maritime security. “Our commitment to ensuring the freedom of navigation and safeguarding global Sea Lines of Communication is backed by a continuous, decades-long operational legacy. Since 2008, the Indian Navy has maintained an uninterrupted, active presence in highly volatile corridors like the Gulf of Aden, without coercion or unilateral actions that undermine the rights of other nations,” he said.Rajnath said India’s emphasis on the rule of law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and its advocacy for freedom of navigation and overflight are not directed against any country but are meant to safeguard the collective interests of all regional stakeholders who depend on open sea lanes and stable maritime governance.
Article Summary: Rajnath Singh underlined that “every strategy of India has been tested, refined and proven in the crucible of real-world operations’ He reaffirmed the country’s commitment to collective regional security and eradication of terrorism in all its forms.

NEW DELHI: The IMD has forecast thunderstorms, lightning, gusty winds and rainfall across several states over the next few days. Heavy to very heavy rainfall is likely in parts of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, the Northeast and southern states, while strong winds and thunderstorms may affect Telangana and neighbouring regions. Meanwhile, a depression over the Bay of Bengal is likely to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm before crossing the Andhra Pradesh coast on November 3.The IMD said the depression over the Bay of Bengal is likely to intensify into a deep depression over the southeast Bay of Bengal by Saturday midnight and further develop into a cyclonic storm on November 1. It is expected to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal on November 2.The system is very likely to cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and Narsapur on the morning of November 3. Wind speeds are expected to reach 100-110 kmph, with gusts of up to 120 kmph.Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam are likely to receive heavy rainfall on November 1, with very heavy rainfall at isolated places on November 2. Gusty winds of 30-40 kmph, reaching up to 50 kmph, are also likely.Delhi is likely to witness partly cloudy skies over the next few days, according to the IMD.No specific rainfall warning for the capital has been mentioned in the forecast.East Uttar Pradesh is likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall on Saturday. The wet spell is expected to continue until November 4.Bihar may receive scattered rainfall over the next few days, with showers likely to continue until November 4.Odisha is likely to witness heavy rainfall on November 3. The IMD has also forecast very heavy rainfall at isolated places on November 2.The impact of Cyclone Arnab and a Western Disturbance has brought light to moderate rainfall to several parts of Himachal Pradesh.Higher-altitude areas, particularly Kinnaur, Shimla and Lahaul-Spiti, may experience conditions favourable for light snowfall. Isolated light rain or snowfall is also possible in higher reaches of Lahaul-Spiti, Kinnaur, Chamba and upper Kangra until November 2.The IMD expects mainly clear weather in the plains and mid-hill districts, including Bilaspur, Mandi, Hamirpur and Una, from November 1 to 3. Temperatures in the plains and mid-hill regions are expected to rise gradually by 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over the next week.Arunachal Pradesh may receive heavy rainfall at isolated places on November 2 and 3.Assam and Meghalaya may experience thunderstorms and lightning in some areas. Heavy rainfall is also likely at isolated places in both states on November 3.East and West Madhya Pradesh are likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall. Gusty winds may also affect parts of the state.Chhattisgarh may experience thunderstorms and lightning. The IMD has forecast heavy rainfall at isolated places on November 2, with another spell likely on November 3 and 4.Vidarbha is likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall. The weather system influencing the region includes a trough extending across Madhya Maharashtra, Marathwada and Vidarbha.Telangana may experience a thundersquall on November 2. Wind speeds are likely to reach 50-60 kmph, with gusts of up to 70 kmph. Thunderstorms and lightning are also possible.Rayalaseema may receive rainfall over the next few days, along with thunderstorms and gusty winds. Wind speeds of 30-40 kmph, reaching up to 50 kmph, are likely.Tamil Nadu is likely to receive rainfall over the next few days. Heavy rainfall is forecast at isolated places on November 3, with showers likely to continue on November 4.Puducherry and Karaikal may receive rainfall over the next few days, according to the IMD.Kerala and Mahe may experience isolated rainfall, with heavy showers likely in parts of the state on November 2 and 3.Coastal Karnataka is likely to witness rainfall from Saturday, with showers expected to continue over the next few days.South Interior Karnataka may receive heavy rainfall on November 2 and 3, while North Interior Karnataka may experience isolated showers.The IMD has forecast light rain and thundershowers at isolated places over the ghats and adjoining areas of North Goa and Kushavati district on November 4 and 5.The rainfall is linked to a trough extending from the east-central Arabian Sea along the Maharashtra coast towards a cyclonic circulation over north Chhattisgarh and adjoining East Madhya Pradesh. The trough passes across Konkan and Goa, Madhya Maharashtra, Marathwada and Vidarbha.Meanwhile, another low-pressure area over the South Andaman Sea is expected to move west-northwestwards and intensify into a depression over the southeast Bay of Bengal around October 31 before moving towards the Andhra Pradesh coast.The remnant of Cyclone Arnab has weakened into a low-pressure area over north Chhattisgarh and adjoining East Madhya Pradesh. The IMD said this system was not affecting the Goa coast.
Article Summary: IMD has forecast thunderstorms, lightning, gusty winds and rainfall across several states over the next few days. Heavy to very heavy rainfall is likely in parts of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, the Northeast and southern states. A depression over the Bay of Bengal is likely to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm before crossing the Andhra coast on November 3.

Article Title: Delhi traffic advisory today ahead of INDIA bloc's Ramlila Maidan rally: Traffic movement to be affected on ITO-Delhi Gate stretch, JLN Marg, Aruna Asaf Ali Road; check roads to avoid, timings and mor
Article Text:
Traffic movement is likely to be affected on several roads, including BSZ Marg (ITO to Delhi Gate), JLN Marg, Aruna Asaf Ali Road, Minto Road, Ranjeet Singh Flyover, Daryaganj-Delhi Gate stretches and Barakhamba Road towards Mandi House.

Traffic restrictions from 10 am to 5 pm

Alternative routes to New Delhi railway station





NEW DELHI: Traffic restrictions and diversions have been imposed across parts of Central Delhi on Sunday as security arrangements were stepped up for the INDIA bloc's 'Chalo Delhi' rally at Ramlila Maidan, where 45,000 to 50,000 people are expected to gather.People started arriving at the venue on Sunday morning, while police personnel were deployed to screen visitors. Door Frame Metal Detectors (DFMDs) have been installed at entry points as part of the security arrangements.Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP), Central, Rohit Rajbir said the venue could accommodate around 45,000 to 50,000 people, adding that arrangements had also been made to manage a larger turnout."We can accommodate a crowd of around 45,000 to 50,000 people here. We expect that if that many arrive, the space will be filled; if more turn up, we will accommodate them on the surrounding roads. A significant portion of the ground is still unoccupied, so most of the people arriving should be able to be accommodated here," he said.He said police personnel had been deployed to screen people entering the venue but clarified that there were no restrictions on movement."We are in touch with the organisers, and they are well aware of the security considerations regarding the rally. I am confident that everything will proceed in accordance with the agreed-upon plan," Rajbir said.RJD chief Lalu Prasad Yadav is among those expected to attend the rally. Top Opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, Mallikarjun Kharge, Mamata Banerjee, Abhishek Banerjee, Hemant Soren, Revanth Reddy, Tejashwi Yadav and Akhilesh Yadav, are also expected to be present.Members of Parliament are expected to assemble at the Constitution Club before proceeding towards Ramlila Maidan from the Minto Road-Connaught Place junction at noon.The Delhi Traffic Police has announced restrictions and diversions across parts of Central Delhi from 10 am to 5 pm and advised commuters to plan their journeys accordingly.Ten diversion points have been identified, including Netaji Subhash Marg T-Point, Rajghat, Delhi Gate, ITO A-Point, Ajmeri Gate Red Light, Ranjeet Singh Flyover near Barakhamba Road, Bhavbhuti Marg-DDU Marg Red Light, Jhandewalan Roundabout, Turkman Gate and Mirdard Chowk.Traffic movement is likely to be affected on several roads, including BSZ Marg (ITO to Delhi Gate), JLN Marg, Aruna Asaf Ali Road, Minto Road, Ranjeet Singh Flyover, Daryaganj-Delhi Gate stretches and Barakhamba Road towards Mandi House.Other affected stretches include KG Marg, Firoz Shah Road, Chelmsford Road and roads around Kamla Market and Hamdard Chowk.Vehicular movement will also be regulated along the stretches from Guru Nanak Chowk to Kamla Market Roundabout, Kamla Market Roundabout to Hamdard Chowk, Hamdard Chowk to Turkman Gate, and Turkman Gate to Guru Nanak Chowk.The movement of Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) buses will be regulated on BSZ Marg, the stretch from Rajghat to JLN Marg, Daryaganj-Delhi Gate Road and Minto Road, depending on prevailing traffic conditions, the advisory said.The traffic police has suggested alternative routes for passengers travelling to New Delhi Railway Station.Those approaching from the Daryaganj Road side have been advised to take Chelmsford Road, the Outer Circle of Connaught Place, Minto Road and Bhavbhuti Marg.Passengers travelling from East Delhi can take the route via ITO, DDU Marg and Bhavbhuti Marg to reach the Ajmeri Gate side of the station.If DDU Marg is disrupted, commuters can use the alternative route via ITO Red Light, W-Point, Sikandra Road, Connaught Place, Paharganj and Chelmsford Road.The traffic police has advised commuters to avoid unnecessary travel towards Astha Kunj Park, Nehru Place and adjoining roads during the programme.Motorists have also been asked to use public transport, preferably the Metro, follow instructions issued by traffic personnel and allow extra time for their journeys.Commuters have been advised against roadside and unauthorised parking near the rally venue.
Article Summary: Traffic restrictions and diversions have been imposed across parts of Central Delhi on Sunday. Security arrangements were stepped up for the INDIA bloc's 'Chalo Delhi' rally at Ramlila Maidan. Door Frame Metal Detectors (DFMDs) have been installed at entry points.
